claim: STOMP is a novel proteomics technique for interrogating micron-scale regions of interest (ROIs) in mammalian tissue, with no requirement for genetic manipulation.
source: Spatially targeted optical microproteomics (STOMP) is a novel proteomics technique for interrogating micron-scale regions of interest (ROIs) in mammalian tissue, with no requirement for genetic manipulation.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the technique.

claim: Methanol or formalin-fixed specimens can be used in STOMP.
source: Methanol or formalin-fixed specimens are stained with fluorescent dyes or antibodies to visualize ROIs, then soaked in solutions containing the photo-tag: 4-benzoylbenzyl-glycyl-hexahistidine.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the types of fixation compatible with STOMP.

claim: STOMP achieves a resolution of 0.67 µm in the xy-plane and 1.48 µm axially.
source: Confocal imaging along with two photon excitation are used to covalently couple photo-tags to all proteins within each ROI, to a resolution of 0.67 µm in the xy-plane and 1.48 µm axially.
evidence: The abstract provides specific resolution measurements.

claim: STOMP can be applied to various biological samples including cell lines, primary cell cultures, ex vivo specimens, biopsy samples, and fixed post-mortem tissue.
source: STOMP can be applied to various biological samples including cell lines, primary cell cultures, ex vivo specimens, biopsy samples, and fixed post-mortem tissue.
evidence: The abstract explicitly lists the types of samples compatible with STOMP.

claim: The silver stain was introduced by Golgi in 1873.
source: Early methods used to identify these deposits include the silver stain introduced by Golgi (1873)
evidence: This is a historical fact cited in the introduction.

claim: Virchow introduced the iodine–sulfuric acid stain for starch.
source: Virchow's iodine–sulfuric acid stain for starch (Virchow, 1854)
evidence: This is a historical fact cited in the introduction.

claim: Virchow coined the term amyloid in 1855.
source: that led to the coining of the term amyloid (Virchow, 1855)
evidence: This is a historical fact cited in the introduction.

claim: Congo red and thioflavin S specifically identify deposits containing amyloid β-pleated sheets.
source: The stains Congo red and thioflavin S (ThS) were discovered later and remain in use (reviewed by Westermark (Sipe and Westermark, 2005) and Tanskanen (Tanskanen, 2013)), specifically identifying deposits containing a particular structural motif: amyloid β-pleated sheets.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The discovery of the prion protein led to the formulation of the protein-only hypothesis of prion disease.
source: Two classic examples include the discovery of the prion protein and formulation of the protein-only hypothesis of prion disease (Bolton et al., 1982)
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by a citation.

claim: The discovery of the Alzheimer amyloid peptide (Aβ) led to the formulation of the amyloid cascade hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease.
source: and the discovery of the Alzheimer amyloid peptide (Aβ) (Glenner and Wong, 1984) and formulation of the amyloid cascade hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD, reviewed by Musiek and Holtzman (Musiek and Holtzman, 2015))
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citations.

claim: TDP-43 is a significant component of ubiquitin-positive intraneuronal inclusions in certain cases of frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: More recently, there was the discovery that the RNA/DNA binding protein TDP-43 (transactive response DNA binding protein 43 kDa) is a significant component of ubiquitin-positive intraneuronal inclusions in certain cases of frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Neumann et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The discovery of TDP-43 helped establish FTD and ALS as spectrum disorders.
source: This discovery helped establish these diseases as spectrum disorders (Mackenzie, 2007)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: TDP-43 mutations are causative for ALS and FTD.
source: it led to the identification of TDP-43 mutations that are causative for ALS and FTD (Sreedharan et al., 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The discovery of TDP-43 established a role for RNA metabolism in ALS/FTD pathogenesis.
source: and established a role for RNA metabolism in ALS/FTD pathogenesis (Lagier-Tourenne and Cleveland, 2009; Mackenzie et al., 2010)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Traditional identification of protein components of pathological deposits involves partial biochemical purification of detergent-insoluble proteins followed by protein sequencing.
source: Identification of the protein components of pathological deposits has traditionally involved the partial biochemical purification of detergent-insoluble proteins present in a tissue specimen followed by protein sequencing.
evidence: This describes traditional methodology.

claim: The discovery of TDP-43 in ubiquitin-positive intraneuronal inclusions required the generation of approximately 1000 monoclonal antibodies.
source: For example, the discovery of TDP-43 in ubiquitin-positive intraneuronal inclusions required the generation of ∼1000 monoclonal antibodies, which were used to screen thousands of tissue sections by immunohistochemistry, to obtain a single monoclonal antibody that specifically labeled ubiquitin-positive intraneuronal inclusions (Neumann et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation describing the methodology used.

claim: Biochemical purification of protein deposits likely loses soluble protein components associated with the core aggregates during fractionation.
source: In addition to being costly and labor intensive, another major limitation of biochemical purification of protein deposits is that soluble protein components associated with the core aggregates are likely to be lost during fractionation.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of biochemical fractionation.

claim: Laser capture microdissection (LCM) can preserve some deposit-associated soluble proteins.
source: A different strategy that can preserve some of the deposit-associated soluble proteins is laser capture microdissection (LCM), in which protein deposits are lifted intact out of sections of the fixed specimen; their protein compositions are then determined by mass spectrometry (Gozal et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The resolution of LCM is approximately 10 µm in the horizontal plane and captures the entire thickness of the tissue section along the vertical axis.
source: The resolution of LCM is ∼10 µm in the horizontal plane and captures the entire thickness of the tissue section along the vertical axis.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of LCM.

claim: When capturing a 3 μm diameter inclusion body with a single 10 µm LCM spot, only approximately 10% of the recovered protein is from the pathology and 90% from the surrounding cellular milieu.
source: For example, when capturing even a relatively large—3 μm in diameter—inclusion body with a single 10 µm LCM spot, only ∼10% of the recovered protein is from the pathology and 90% from the surrounding cellular milieu.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the geometry of LCM capture.

claim: LCM has proven useful in the proteomic analysis of systemic amyloidosis, where the amyloid deposits are very large with feature size typically approximately 50,000 μm2 in area.
source: LCM has nevertheless proven useful, however, in the proteomic analysis of systemic amyloidosis, where the amyloid deposits are very large and the feature size is typically ∼50,000 μm2 in area (Sethi et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Mass spectrometry imaging can provide spatially resolved mass spectrometry analysis achieving 1 mm–10 μm resolution.
source: Mass spectrometry imaging and its variants can also provide spatially resolved mass spectrometry analysis by directly coupling imaging with laser ablation and achieving 1 mm–10 μm resolution (Stoeckli et al., 2001; Wiseman et al., 2006; Wucher et al., 2007)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Mass spectrometry imaging is usually used to look for specific targets rather than in discovery mode.
source: but it is usually used to look for specific targets rather than in discovery mode.
evidence: This describes a limitation of mass spectrometry imaging.

claim: Proximity labeling techniques such as Bio-ID and APEX have been used to elucidate the composition of several difficult to purify organelles.
source: Recently, proximity labeling techniques such as Bio-ID and APEX have provided high spatial resolution to mass spectrometry, and these techniques have been used to elucidate the composition of several difficult to purify organelles (Roux et al., 2012; Rhee et al., 2013; Firat-Karalar et al., 2014; Hung et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Proximity labeling relies on genetic manipulations to express an exogenous fusion protein to label adjacent components.
source: However, proximity labeling relies on genetic manipulations to express an exogenous fusion protein to label adjacent components; this protein must be specifically and accurately targeted into a particular biological structure.
evidence: This describes a requirement of proximity labeling techniques.

claim: Imperfect localization in proximity labeling results in selective labeling of neighbors outside of the target region yielding false positive associations.
source: Imperfect localization, especially in rare structures, results in selective labeling of neighbors outside of the target region yielding false positive associations.
evidence: This describes a limitation of proximity labeling.

claim: Early LCM studies utilizing 2D gel electrophoresis coupled with mass spectrometry detected a modest number of plaque-associated proteins.
source: Early LCM studies utilizing 2D gel electrophoresis coupled with mass spectrometry have detected a modest number of plaque-associated proteins, including an assortment of proteins associated with cell signaling, chaperone function, membrane trafficking, and proteolysis (Liao et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: A recent LCM study suggested that amyloid plaques in AD are highly homogenous structures composed almost exclusively of Aβ.
source: A more recent LCM study has suggested that amyloid plaques in AD are highly homogenous structures that are composed almost exclusively of Aβ (Söderberg et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Sample washing steps with 1% SDS may strip away soluble plaque-associated proteins in LCM studies.
source: The latter study, however, employed sample washing steps with 1% SDS, which may strip away soluble plaque-associated proteins.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of the washing procedure.

claim: A study examining the sarkosyl-insoluble fraction of brain samples from patients with AD identified altered levels of eleven specific proteins.
source: Finally, a recent attempt to capture more plaque-associated proteins potentially lost to LCM examined the sarkosyl-insoluble fraction of brain samples from patients with AD and appropriate controls (Gozal et al., 2009). Altered levels of eleven specific proteins were identified by this approach but colocalization with amyloid plaques was difficult to validate in many cases
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Not all insoluble proteins within the brain will necessarily originate from senile plaques.
source: not all insoluble proteins within the brain will necessarily originate from senile plaques.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of biochemical fractionation.

claim: The post-synaptic protein IRSp53 was highly down-regulated in AD.
source: A recent proteomic analysis of fractions obtained from differential centrifugation procedures that yield fractions enriched in post-synaptic proteins have demonstrated that the post-synaptic protein IRSp53 was highly down-regulated in AD (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: STOMP combines two-photon laser scanning microscopy with photochemical affinity labeling and mass spectrometry.
source: We have developed a semi-automated technique called spatially targeted optical microproteomics (STOMP), which combines two-photon laser scanning microscopy with photochemical affinity labeling and mass spectrometry.
evidence: This describes the components of the STOMP technique.

claim: Two-photon excitation has previously been used to drive microscopic, 3D-resolved photochemistry.
source: While two-photon excitation has previously been used to drive microscopic, 3D-resolved photochemistry (Lee et al., 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: STOMP represents the first application of two-photon excitation to affinity photolabeling.
source: STOMP represents the first application of this technique to affinity photolabeling
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of STOMP.

claim: STOMP offers single-micron-scale three-dimensional resolution that is an order of magnitude better than LCM.
source: offering single-micron-scale three-dimensional resolution that is an order of magnitude better than the current state of the art LCM.
evidence: This is a comparison of STOMP resolution to LCM.

claim: The photo-affinity ligand used in STOMP is a peptide of sequence: 4-benzoylbenzyl-Gly-His-His-His-His-His-His-CONH2 (6HisBP).
source: The photo-affinity ligand or photo-tag used here is a peptide of sequence: 4-benzoylbenzyl-Gly-His-His-His-His-His-His-CONH2 (6HisBP) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the chemical structure of the photo-tag, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Benzoylbenzene is a photoreactive group that forms covalent bonds with C–H and N–H groups upon excitation.
source: Benzoylbenzene is a photoreactive group that forms covalent bonds with C–H and N–H groups upon excitation.
evidence: This describes the chemical properties of the photoreactive group.

claim: The 6HisBP photo-tag molecule has a molecular mass of 1105 Da.
source: The 6HisBP photo-tag molecule (molecular mass, 1105 Da)
evidence: This provides the molecular mass of the photo-tag.

claim: Congo red has a molecular mass of 697 Da.
source: is of similar size to Congo red (molecular mass, 697 Da)
evidence: This provides the molecular mass of Congo red for comparison.

claim: 6HisBP should have a similar ability to penetrate biological specimens as Congo red.
source: is of similar size to Congo red (molecular mass, 697 Da) and should have a similar ability to penetrate biological specimens.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar molecular sizes.

claim: The specimen is fixed and permeabilized in methanol in the STOMP procedure.
source: The specimen is fixed and permeabilized in methanol, then protein deposits in the specimen are selectively stained using antibodies or specific fluorescent dyes.
evidence: This describes a step in the STOMP protocol.

claim: The wavelength of the confocal laser is in the visible range and does not excite the UV-absorbing photo-tag.
source: The wavelength of the confocal laser is in the visible range and does not excite the UV-absorbing photo-tag.
evidence: This describes a technical aspect of the imaging procedure.

claim: Two-photon microscopy can excite a small volume (<1 µm3) anywhere in the specimen.
source: Two-photon microscopy can excite a small volume (<1 µm3, Figures 1A and Figure 2) anywhere in the specimen
evidence: This describes the capability of two-photon microscopy, with reference to figures.

claim: Conventional confocal microscopy excites a continuous cone that spans the entire thickness of the specimen.
source: while conventional confocal microscopy excites a continuous cone that spans the entire thickness of the specimen, which would result in the covalent attachment of the photo-tag to off-target regions.
evidence: This describes a limitation of conventional confocal microscopy for this application.

claim: Unlike LCM, no manual tracing of features is required with STOMP.
source: Importantly, unlike LCM, no manual tracing of features is required with STOMP.
evidence: This describes an advantage of STOMP over LCM.

claim: Histidine-rich proteins ubiquitous in all mammalian tissues represent potential contaminants that could bind the nickel affinity beads.
source: Histidine-rich proteins ubiquitous in all mammalian tissues represent potential contaminants that could bind the nickel affinity beads and confound the STOMP analysis.
evidence: This describes a potential problem in the STOMP procedure.

claim: Limited treatment of tissue sections with dilute diethyl pyrocarbonate (DEPC) covalently modifies histidyl residues and abolishes their ability to bind nickel.
source: To circumvent this problem, the first step of the procedure involves limited treatment of the tissue sections with dilute diethyl pyrocarbonate (DEPC). DEPC covalently modifies histidyl residues that abolishes their ability to bind nickel (Wallis and Holbrook, 1973).
evidence: This describes a step in the STOMP protocol to prevent non-specific binding, supported by a citation.

claim: The width (FWHM) of the phototagged volume was measured at 0.67 µm along the x and y axes, and 1.48 µm along the z axis.
source: We measured the diameter (full width at half-maximum, FWHM) of the phototagged volume at 0.67 µm along the x and y axes, and 1.48 µm along the z axis (Figure 2).
evidence: This provides measured resolution data, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Taking the excited region to be an ellipsoid, the total volume of a single spot is 0.38 µm3.
source: Taking the excited region to be an ellipsoid, the total volume of a single spot is 0.38 µm3.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured dimensions.

claim: TgCRND8 mice express a human form of the amyloid precursor protein carrying two mutations associated with familial AD.
source: We used TgCRND8 mice, a well-characterized transgenic mouse model of AD (Chishti et al., 2001), as a model system for the development of the STOMP technique. These mice express a human form of the amyloid precursor protein carrying two mutations associated with familial AD
evidence: This describes the mouse model used, supported by a citation.

claim: TgCRND8 mice produce amyloid plaques and exhibit spatial learning impairments by 3 months of age.
source: and they produce amyloid plaques and exhibit spatial learning impairments by 3 months of age.
evidence: This describes the phenotype of the mouse model.

claim: The study used frozen sections (post-fixed in methanol) of the brains from TgCRND8 mice of 8 months of age.
source: This study used frozen sections (post-fixed in methanol) of the brains known to contain plaques, from TgCRND8 mice of 8 months of age.
evidence: This describes the sample preparation.

claim: Two-photon excitation light photo-bleaches the ThS fluorophores present in regions of the specimen targeted by the mask.
source: This excitation light has two effects. First, and most importantly, it photo-activates 6HisBP molecules that are in the amyloid deposits causing photo-tagging of constituent proteins. Second, it serendipitously photo-bleaches the ThS fluorophores present in regions of the specimen targeted by the mask.
evidence: This describes an observed effect of the two-photon excitation.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining of the tissue section with anti-His6 antibody after photo-activation superimposes on the digital mask, highlighting the very high accuracy of targeting of the two-photon laser.
source: Immunofluorescence staining of the tissue section with anti-His6 antibody after photo-activation superimposes on the digital mask, thus highlighting the very high accuracy of targeting of the two-photon laser (Figure 1C3).
evidence: This describes validation of the targeting accuracy, with reference to Figure 1C3.

claim: The dark control sample shows very few bands in the silver-stain gel from material bound to the Ni-NTA beads compared to the STOMP sample.
source: The dark control sample, which—aside from two-photon excitation—was treated identically to the STOMP sample, was run alongside the STOMP sample. It shows very few bands in the silver-stain gel from material bound to the nickel-nitrilotriacetic acid (Ni-NTA) beads compared to the STOMP sample
evidence: This describes the results of the control experiment, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Nonspecific photo-tagging and nonspecific binding of proteins to the nickel affinity beads is minimal.
source: confirming that nonspecific photo-tagging and nonspecific binding of proteins to the nickel affinity beads is minimal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control experiment data.

claim: The STOMP sample contains large amounts of a low molecular weight protein that was subsequently identified as Aβ (4.5 kDa).
source: In addition to a number of proteins ranging in molecular weight from 20 kDa to >250 kDa, the STOMP sample contains large amounts of a low molecular weight protein that was subsequently identified as Aβ (4.5 kDa) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes a finding from the gel electrophoresis, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The total volume of tissue that needs to be photo-tagged to obtain sufficient material for mass spectrometry analysis is approximately 2 × 106 µm3.
source: In this study, we were able to identify proteins present in relative abundance in the pathological feature being examined using a total photo-tagged volume of approximately 2 × 106 µm3.
evidence: This describes the amount of tissue required for the analysis.

claim: Two frozen sections of TgCRND8 brain tissue were sufficient to produce the necessary volume of photo-tagged tissue required for one STOMP experiment.
source: Two frozen sections of TgCRND8 brain tissue were sufficient to produce the necessary volume of photo-tagged tissue required for one STOMP experiment
evidence: This describes the sample requirements.

claim: The STOMP process required a total of 12–16 hr of microscope time per sample (6–8 hr per section).
source: and the process required a total of 12–16 hr of microscope time per sample (6–8 hr per section).
evidence: This describes the time requirements for the procedure.

claim: Regions of interest (ROIs) as small as 0.38 µm can be analyzed using STOMP.
source: Based on our determination of the resolution of STOMP, regions of interest (ROIs) as small as 0.38 µm can be analyzed (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on the measured resolution, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The technical replicates of the proteomic analyses demonstrate a very high degree of correlation (r2 = 0.98).
source: The technical replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) demonstrate a very high degree of correlation (r2 = 0.98)
evidence: This describes the reproducibility of the technique, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The biological replicates demonstrate significant overlap in proteins identified.
source: and the biological replicates demonstrate significant overlap in proteins identified (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the reproducibility of the technique, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The most abundant protein found in STOMP from TgCRND8 mouse plaques was Aβ.
source: As expected, the most abundant protein found in STOMP from TgCRND8 mouse plaques was Aβ (Figure 1D, Table 1).
evidence: This describes the primary finding, with reference to Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: 454 proteins were identified in at least one of two biological replicates from TgCRND8 mouse plaques.
source: In addition to Aβ, we identified 454 proteins in at least one of two biological replicates (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the number of proteins identified.

claim: 62 proteins were found with probability >0.8 of being associated with the plaques using the SAINT algorithm.
source: We found 62 proteins with probability >0.8 of being found associated with the plaques
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: 146 proteins were found with probability >0.5 of being associated with the plaques using the SAINT algorithm.
source: and 146 with probability >0.5 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Synaptosomal proteins were highly enriched in TgCRND8 mouse plaques, including SNAP25, VAMP2, v-ATPase, and synapsins 1 and 2.
source: Among these, synaptosomal proteins were highly enriched, including SNAP25, vesicle-associated membrane protein 2 (VAMP2), vesicular proton pump ATPase (v-ATPase), and synapsins 1 and 2.
evidence: This describes a category of proteins found in the plaques.

claim: Apolipoprotein E was detected in TgCRND8 mouse plaques at a SAINT score of 0.70.
source: Apolipoprotein E, which is sometimes associated with senile plaques (Thal et al., 1997), was also detected, albeit at a SAINT score of 0.70 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes a specific protein found, with a citation for context.

claim: Certain common synaptic markers—including chromogranin A/C, synaptophysin, synaptogyrin I, synaptoporin, α-synuclein, and VGLUT1 and 2—were not detected in TgCRND8 mouse plaques.
source: Certain common synaptic markers—including chromogranin A/C, synaptophysin, synaptogyrin I, synaptoporin, α-synuclein, and VGLUT1 and 2—were not detected in the plaques.
evidence: This describes proteins that were not found in the plaques.

claim: The plaques were devoid of uniquely post-synaptic proteins.
source: Interestingly, the plaques were also devoid of uniquely post-synaptic proteins.
evidence: This describes a category of proteins not found in the plaques.

claim: Many mitochondrial proteins were identified in TgCRND8 mouse plaques.
source: We also identified many mitochondrial proteins
evidence: This describes a category of proteins found in the plaques.

claim: The intrinsic hydrophobicity of mitochondrial membrane proteins may predispose them to associate with amyloid plaques.
source: although the reason for this is unclear, it may be that the intrinsic hydrophobicity of mitochondrial membrane proteins may predispose them to associate with amyloid plaques.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the presence of mitochondrial proteins.

claim: VAMP2, synapsin 1, and dynamin 1 are present in both plaque and non-plaque STOMP analysis but are significantly greater enriched in the plaque STOMP samples.
source: Comparison with proteins found from STOMP analysis of non-plaque areas revealed only limited overlap (Supplementary file 2); VAMP2, synapsin 1, and dynamin 1 are present in both plaque and non-plaque STOMP analysis but are significantly greater enriched in the plaque STOMP samples.
evidence: This describes a comparison between plaque and non-plaque samples.

claim: Aβ, SNAP25, VAMP2, v-ATPase, synapsin 1, and ApoE were found to be present and are apparently genuine components of the amyloid plaque in TgCRND8 mice.
source: Using confocal microscopy, we examined colocalization of ThS-positive plaques with immunfluorescently labeled Aβ, SNAP25, VAMP2, v-ATPase, synapsin 1, and ApoE. All were found to be present and are apparently genuine components of the amyloid plaque (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes validation by immunofluorescence, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Optical sectioning demonstrates the presence of Aβ, SNAP25, VAMP2, v-ATPase, synapsin 1, and ApoE in the core of the amyloid plaques suggesting they were incorporated at the earliest stages of plaque formation.
source: Optical sectioning demonstrates the presence of each of these proteins in the core of the amyloid plaques suggesting they were incorporated at the earliest stages of plaque formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data.

claim: Staining of SNAP25, VAMP2, and v-ATPase reveal an immunopositive halo surrounding each of the plaques indicating an accumulation of these proteins not only in the amyloid core but also in the vicinity of the plaques.
source: Staining of SNAP25, VAMP2, and v-ATPase reveal an immunopositive halo surrounding each of the plaques indicating an accumulation of these proteins not only in the amyloid core but also in the vicinity of the plaques
evidence: This describes an observation from immunofluorescence staining, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Synapsin 1 immunostaining did not have a halo surrounding the plaques.
source: interestingly, synapsin 1 immunostaining did not have this halo.
evidence: This describes a difference in staining pattern.

claim: Immunostaining of syntaxin 1, synaptophysin, and α-synuclein confirmed that these proteins are not concentrated in the amyloid plaques in TgCRND8 mice.
source: Immunostaining of some of these markers, syntaxin 1, synaptophysin, and α-synuclein, confirmed that these proteins are not concentrated in the amyloid plaques (Figure 4).
evidence: This describes validation by immunostaining, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: α-Synuclein has been reported to be associated with senile plaques in human patients with AD.
source: α-Synuclein has been reported to be associated with senile plaques in human patients with AD
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings.

claim: TgCRND8 mice are known to not accumulate α-synuclein in their plaques.
source: however, TgCRND8 mice are known to not accumulate α-synuclein in their plaques (Xu et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: One possibility is that damaged dystrophic neurites that are known to surround the plaques are spilling their contents and the physical properties of certain pre-synaptic proteins cause them to bind with especially high affinity to amyloid plaques.
source: One possibility is that damaged dystrophic neurites that are known to surround the plaques (Chishti et al., 2001) are spilling their contents and the physical properties of certain pre-synaptic proteins cause them to bind with especially high affinity to amyloid plaques.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the findings, with a citation for context.

claim: Many of the pre-synaptic proteins found in plaques are membrane proteins with coiled coil domains.
source: In this regard, it is noteworthy that many of these proteins are membrane proteins with coiled coil domains (Takamori et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Aβ fibrils and/or oligomers may bind directly to synaptic vesicles and interfere with synaptic function.
source: Another possibility, which is not mutually exclusive and provides an explanation for the presence of pre-synaptic proteins in plaques, is that Aβ fibrils and/or oligomers bind directly to synaptic vesicles and interfere with synaptic function.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the findings.

claim: Evidence for a damaging effect of Aβ on synapses and dendrites has been available for some time.
source: Evidence for a damaging effect of Aβ on synapses and dendrites has been available for some time (Mattson et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Diffusible Aβ oligomers added to cultured primary neurons have been shown to associate with synaptosomes and a concomitant synaptic deterioration is observed.
source: Diffusible Aβ oligomers added to cultured primary neurons have been shown to associate with synaptosomes and a concomitant synaptic deterioration is observed (Lacor et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: In post-mortem AD tissue and in transgenic AD mice, an inverse correlation between levels of Aβ oligomers and levels of synaptic proteins was noted.
source: In post-mortem AD tissue and in transgenic AD mice, an inverse correlation between levels of Aβ oligomers and levels of synaptic proteins was noted (Pham et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The reduction in the levels of detectable synaptic protein in AD tissue may be the result of the aggregation and entrapment of the synaptic proteins in the amyloid plaques.
source: The reduction in the levels of detectable synaptic protein in AD tissue may be the result of the aggregation and entrapment of the synaptic proteins in the amyloid plaques.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the findings.

claim: The STOMP technique has provided clear evidence of interaction of amyloid plaques with pre-synaptic proteins.
source: In sum, the STOMP technique has provided clear evidence of interaction of amyloid plaques with pre-synaptic proteins.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data.

claim: Human tissue is inherently more difficult to work with than animal tissue because of biochemical changes associated with post-mortem degradation.
source: Human tissue is inherently more difficult to work with than animal tissue because of biochemical changes associated with post-mortem degradation.
evidence: This is a general statement about working with human tissue.

claim: Formalin causes covalent modification of proteins and confounds mass spectrometry analysis.
source: Furthermore, formalin, the fixative of choice for human tissue, causes covalent modification of proteins and confounds mass spectrometry analysis.
evidence: This describes a technical challenge with formalin-fixed tissue.

claim: The STOMP technique is suitable for the analysis of formalin-fixed post-mortem human tissue.
source: These limitations notwithstanding, we find the STOMP technique is suitable for the analysis of formalin-fixed post-mortem human tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful application to human tissue.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis of senile plaques from a severe case of AD identified 60 proteins that were statistically significantly enriched, with Aβ being the most abundant protein component.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis of the protein composition of these senile plaques identified 60 proteins that were statistically significantly enriched, with Aβ being the most abundant protein component (Table 2).
evidence: This describes the results from human AD tissue, with reference to Table 2.

claim: Synaptic proteins and proteins involved in synaptic vesicle transport comprised 15% of the abundant protein component of the plaques in human AD tissue.
source: Synaptic proteins and proteins involved in synaptic vesicle transport comprised 15% of the abundant protein component of the plaques.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the protein composition.

claim: GFAP and SNAP25 were detected by both STOMP and immunofluorescence in human AD senile plaques.
source: For validation of the STOMP analysis of senile plaques, immunofluorescence staining was employed, revealing that GFAP and SNAP25 were detected by both immunofluorescence
evidence: This describes validation results, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Tau and α-synuclein were not detected by either STOMP or immunofluorescence in human AD senile plaques.
source: while tau and α-synuclein were not detected by either technique (Figure 5).
evidence: This describes validation results, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Gliosis is a well-known feature of AD, and reactive glial cells are often found surrounding amyloid plaques.
source: Gliosis is a well-known feature of AD, and reactive glial cells are often found surrounding amyloid plaques (Mandybur and Chuirazzi, 1990; Sofroniew and Vinters, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Glial proteins, GFAP and EAAT, were both detected in human senile plaques.
source: Glial proteins, GFAP and excitatory amino acid transporter (EAAT) (Anderson and Swanson, 2000), were both detected in (human) senile plaques (Table 2)
evidence: This describes findings from human tissue, with a citation for context and reference to Table 2.

claim: Only EAAT was detected in TgCRND8 amyloid plaques.
source: however, only EAAT was detected in TgCRND8 amyloid plaques (Table 1)
evidence: This describes findings from mouse tissue, with reference to Table 1.

claim: Astrocytes are more intimately associated with amyloid plaques in human tissue compared to plaques in the TgCRND mouse.
source: This apparent discrepancy is likely due to astrocytes being more intimately associated with amyloid plaques in human tissue (Figure 5A,E,I) compared to plaques in the TgCRND mouse (Figure 4D,J,P).
evidence: This is an inference based on immunofluorescence data, with references to Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Tau protein was not among the abundant plaque proteins in human AD tissue.
source: Tau protein was also not among the abundant plaque proteins.
evidence: This describes a finding from the STOMP analysis.

claim: Tau, which is contained in dystrophic neurites that surround the plaques, do not occupy the same physical space as the plaques and were hence not detected in the STOMP analysis.
source: Immunofluorescence staining shows that tau, which is contained in dystrophic neurites that surround the plaques, do not occupy the same physical space as the plaques and were hence not detected in the STOMP analysis (Figure 3B,H,N).
evidence: This explains why tau was not detected, with reference to Figure 3 (note: the text says Figure 3 but likely means Figure 5 based on context).

claim: SNAP25 was detected in the STOMP analysis and was seen to colocalize with senile plaques in human AD tissue.
source: SNAP25, on the other hand, was detected in the STOMP analysis and was seen to colocalize with senile plaques (Figure 5D,H,L)
evidence: This describes validation by immunofluorescence, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: α-synuclein is part of the NAC (non-amyloid components) of plaques—with a possible role in fibril formation but not part of the plaque core.
source: α-synuclein is part of the NAC (non-amyloid components) of plaques—with a possible role in fibril formation but not part of the plaque core (Culvenor et al., 1999; Wirths and Bayer, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: α-synuclein was found not to be enriched in the plaques of this case of AD as detected by both STOMP analysis and immunofluorescent staining.
source: These proteins were found not to be enriched in the plaques of this case of AD as detected by both STOMP analysis (Table 2) or by immunofluorescent staining (Figure 5C,G,K).
evidence: This describes findings from both STOMP and immunofluorescence, with references to Table 2 and Figure 5.

claim: Senile plaques in the human AD tissue were positive for both SNAP25 and VAMP2.
source: Senile plaques in the human AD tissue were positive for both SNAP25 and VAMP2.
evidence: This describes immunohistochemical findings, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Synaptophysin staining displayed a unique punctate lobular profile that decorated the periphery of the plaque in the human tissue.
source: However, synaptophysin staining, which was absent in the amyloid deposits of AD mice, displayed a unique punctate lobular profile that decorated the periphery of the plaque in the human tissue (Figure 6).
evidence: This describes a difference between mouse and human tissue, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: STOMP analyses demonstrate the molecular differences of amyloid deposits in AD mice compared to senile plaques in AD patients.
source: These STOMP analyses demonstrate the molecular differences of amyloid deposits in AD mice compared to senile plaques in AD patients
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparative data.

claim: STOMP analyses confirm the segregation of pre-synaptic proteins in and around amyloid plaques and point to their potential importance in AD pathophysiology.
source: but confirm the segregation of these pre-synaptic proteins in and around amyloid plaques and point to their potential importance in AD pathophysiology.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data.

claim: Some proteins identified by STOMP (including v-ATPase, dynamin, SNAP25, VAMP2, synapsin, clathrin, ankyrin, and so on) were detected in previous LCM-based studies.
source: Some proteins identified by STOMP (including v-ATPase, dynamin, SNAP25, VAMP2, synapsin, clathrin, ankyrin, and so on; see Tables 1, 2 and Supplementary file 3) were detected in previous LCM-based studies
evidence: This compares STOMP findings to previous studies.

claim: With the exception of v-ATPase and dynamin, proteins identified by STOMP were not previously shown to be significantly or sufficiently enriched compared to the control samples in LCM studies.
source: however, with the exception of v-ATPase and dynamin, these proteins were not previously shown to be significantly or sufficiently enriched compared to the control samples (Liao et al., 2004).
evidence: This compares STOMP findings to previous studies, with a citation.

claim: The highly specific nature of STOMP protein labeling and recovery permits very sensitive detection of proteins present in plaques, even if those proteins are also abundant in the remainder of the brain.
source: The highly specific nature of STOMP protein labeling and recovery permits very sensitive detection of proteins present in plaques, even if those proteins are also abundant in the remainder of the brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the advantages of STOMP.

claim: The discovery that there is an accumulation of certain pre-synaptic proteins in AD plaques and in TgCRND8 mice provides direct evidence for an association between amyloid plaque formation and synaptic function.
source: Our discovery that there is an accumulation of certain pre-synaptic proteins in AD plaques and in TgCRND8 mice provides direct evidence for an association between amyloid plaque formation and synaptic function.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the findings.

claim: STOMP of formalin-fixed archival tissue is possible.
source: While our initial work in characterizing amyloid deposits in mouse brain used methanol fixed tissues to minimize problems with solubilizing tissue, our experience with human AD pathological tissue shows that STOMP of formalin-fixed archival tissue is possible.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful application to human tissue.

claim: The STOMP technique is ideally suited for determination of the compositions of intracellular protein inclusions seen in ALS and FTD.
source: The STOMP technique is ideally suited for determination of the compositions of intracellular protein inclusions seen in ALS and FTD.
evidence: This is a statement about potential applications of STOMP.

claim: The principle components of ALS and FTD inclusions, such as TDP-43, FUS, and dipeptide repeat proteins are known.
source: While the principle components of these inclusions, such as TDP-439, FUS (Kwiatkowski et al., 2009; Vance et al., 2009), and dipeptide repeat proteins (Mori et al., 2013) are known
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Determination of the secondary components of ALS and FTD inclusions could shed light on disease etiology.
source: determination of the secondary components of the inclusions could shed light on disease etiology.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential insights.

claim: The nonspecific nature of benzophenone photochemistry should cause photo-tagging of nonprotein components as well.
source: In developing the STOMP technique, we have focused on identification of photo-tagged proteins, however, the nonspecific nature of benzophenone photochemistry should cause photo-tagging of nonprotein components as well.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chemistry of the photo-tag.

claim: The STOMP technique can easily be modified to identify the RNA composition of biological features.
source: In this regard, the STOMP technique can easily be modified to identify the RNA composition of biological features.
evidence: This is a statement about potential modifications of STOMP.

claim: RNA-containing subcellular structures such as P-bodies and stress granules have been implicated in neurodegenerative disease.
source: RNA-containing subcellular structures such as P-bodies and stress granules have been implicated in neurodegenerative disease (Li et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: P-bodies and stress granules are of suitable size for STOMP.
source: these structures are of suitable size for STOMP
evidence: This is an inference based on the size of these structures and STOMP resolution.

claim: There is a realistic possibility of determining jointly the proteomic and transcriptomic composition of P-bodies and stress granules with STOMP.
source: and there is a realistic possibility of determining jointly their proteomic and transcriptomic composition with this technique.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: The application of STOMP to many other aspects of cell biology research is conceivable.
source: The application of this technique to many other aspects of cell biology research is also conceivable.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: TgCRND8 mice express a transgene that encodes human amyloid precursor protein (APP695) harboring both the 'Swedish' double mutation KM670/671/NL and the additional 'Indiana' point mutation V717F.
source: Transgenic CRND8 (TgCRND8) mice express a transgene that encodes human amyloid precursor protein (APP695) harboring both the 'Swedish' double mutation KM670/671/NL and the additional 'Indiana' point mutation V717F
evidence: This describes the genetic modifications in the mouse model.

claim: TgCRND8 mice develop dense-cored amyloid plaques and neuritic pathology by 5 months of age.
source: they develop dense-cored amyloid plaques and neuritic pathology by 5 months of age (Chishti et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Animals were sacrificed at 8 months and their brains were embedded in OCT medium for frozen sectioning onto glass slides.
source: Animals were sacrificed at 8 months and their brains were embedded in OCT medium for frozen sectioning onto glass slides.
evidence: This describes the sample preparation method.

claim: Sections were post-fixed by immersion for 10 min in −20°C methanol, air dried at room temperature, and stored at −70°C.
source: Sections were post-fixed by immersion for 10 min in −20°C methanol, air dried at room temperature, and stored at −70°C.
evidence: This describes the sample preparation method.

claim: All experiments were performed in accordance with the guidelines imposed by the University of Toronto Animal Care Committee and Canadian Council for Animal Care.
source: All experiments were performed in accordance with the guidelines imposed by the University of Toronto Animal Care Committee and Canadian Council for Animal Care.
evidence: This describes ethical compliance.

claim: Microscopy employed Zeiss LSM 510 and LSM 710 confocal microscopes, equipped with two-photon infrared (Coherent Chameleon, tuned to 720 nm) laser sources.
source: Microscopy employed Zeiss LSM 510 and LSM 710 confocal microscopes, equipped with two-photon infrared (Coherent Chameleon, tuned to 720 nm) laser sources.
evidence: This describes the equipment used.

claim: ThS fluorescence was excited at 488 nm and imaged confocally through 505 nm longpass or 500–530 nm bandpass filters.
source: ThS fluorescence was excited at 488 nm and imaged confocally through 505 nm longpass or 500–530 nm bandpass filters.
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters.

claim: The nominal pixel spacing was 0.44 × 0.44 µm using a 20× 1.20 NA water immersion objective lens.
source: The nominal pixel spacing was 0.44 .44× 0.44 µm using a 20× 1.20 NA water immersion objective lens.
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters.

claim: Each pixel in the mask image was irradiated six times, for 4 ms on each pass.
source: Using a custom macro for controlling the two-photon microscope (Pham et al., 2007) each pixel in the mask image was irradiated six times, for 4 ms on each pass.
evidence: This describes the photo-tagging parameters, with a citation for the macro.

claim: The total volume photo-activated was approximately 2 × 106 µm3 per sample (1 × 106 μm3 per section).
source: The total volume photo-activated was approximately 2 × 106 µm3 per sample (1 × 106 μm3 per section).
evidence: This describes the amount of tissue photo-tagged.

claim: For methanol-fixed murine tissue, 200 μl of solubilization buffer containing 2% SDS, 8 M urea, 250 mM NaCl, 10 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.2), 10% (wt/vol) glycerol, and 2% β-ME was added to each tube.
source: For methanol-fixed murine tissue, 200 μl of solubilization buffer containing 2% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS, Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA), 8 M urea, 250 mM NaCl, 10 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.2), 10% (wt/vol) glycerol, and 2% β-ME was added to each tube.
evidence: This describes the solubilization protocol.

claim: For solubilization of formalin-fixed human tissue, 400 µl of a modified solubilization buffer containing 200 mM Tris (in addition to the ingredients noted above, as a formaldehyde scavenger) was used.
source: For solubilization of formalin-fixed human tissue, 400 µl of a modified solubilization buffer containing 200 mM Tris (in addition to the ingredients noted above, as a formaldehyde scavenger) was used.
evidence: This describes the modified solubilization protocol for formalin-fixed tissue.

claim: Formalin-fixed sections were held at 90°C for 60 min.
source: Formalin-fixed sections were held at 90°C for 60 min.
evidence: This describes the solubilization protocol for formalin-fixed tissue.

claim: Tissues from AD cases were collected with patient consent and handled under protocols approved by the University Health Network.
source: Tissues from AD cases were collected with patient consent and handled under protocols approved by the University Health Network.
